output:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, I am sorry to keep you up at this hour. Take your time. Tell me what you can about the evening.

FÉLIX: I cannot think of it as one evening. It comes back in pieces. Rosa's face in the hall. The cold coming in under the door. My aunt standing very straight by the stairs. Forgive me, Inspector. I make jokes when I am frightened. It is a bad habit I have had since I was a boy.

MATTHEY: Start at dinner, then. Tell me as you remember it.

FÉLIX: My uncle made us all bring our watches to the table, as he does every year. When the temple struck nine, I took mine out, and it showed twenty minutes to nine. My uncle made a scene about it in front of everyone. He told me what was wrong with it, and he said it loudly, so that Girard laughed.

MATTHEY: Whose watch is it?

FÉLIX: It was my father's. Jules. He died in 1889, and it has been mine since. Nobody has ever been allowed to touch it, not even my uncle. He asked me often enough to let him regulate it. I never did. I suppose he never forgave me for that.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library and stayed there alone. I poured myself a brandy, and then another. I know how that looks too. I was alone on the floor directly below his atelier, drinking my uncle's brandy while he sat upstairs with his repeater. I know exactly how that looks.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you remember of the time.

FÉLIX: When the temple struck ten, my watch showed twenty to ten. I had been looking at the clock on the library mantel, and I thought it was earlier than I expected. I cannot say more than that.

MATTHEY: Go on.

FÉLIX: I heard someone go quickly up the stairs, past the library door, at a quarter past ten by my watch. I did not see who it was. The door was shut. Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, someone came quickly down. Again I did not see who. I only heard the feet on the stairs.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else before the next thing?

FÉLIX: My aunt's piano was playing downstairs. Chopin, I think. She plays Chopin when she is troubled, though I would not have said she was troubled tonight. Then, at eighteen minutes past ten by my watch, I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. And then my uncle's repeater sounded. I counted the first notes without meaning to. Ten slow deep notes. Then some doubled notes. Then quick high ones, and I stopped counting. When the thump came, my aunt's piano was still playing.

MATTHEY: Thank you. And later?

FÉLIX: At thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch, Bastien Girard came into the library. He had come to talk about the repeater, he said, and about the price, which they had quarrelled over at dinner. We sat together there until the temple struck eleven. I poured him a brandy. He did not drink it.

MATTHEY: Why did Monsieur Girard want to see you?

FÉLIX: I owe him money, Inspector. Not a small sum. He has been patient, more patient than I deserve. He is a hard man in business, but he is not a fool, and he knows I cannot pay him back out of my own pocket. My uncle's estate would have settled it, I suppose. I had begun to think of that as my future.

MATTHEY: What did the repeater mean to your uncle?

FÉLIX: Everything. Four years of his life on one watch. He meant it to strike the first minute of the new century, and he would talk of nothing else at dinner for months. He used to say it was the only thing in the house that did exactly what it was told.
